kurz: How banks got into crisis without bad loans, why the returns on the wave of investment in artificial intelligence are not yet assured, and why interest rates are rising again in 2026.

bloecke.md:
The banking crisis of March 2023 did not start with bad loans. Silicon Valley Bank failed because of US Treasury bonds and government-guaranteed mortgage securities whose default risk was practically zero. The losses arose from the second type of risk inherent in every fixed-income security. When market interest rates rise, the prices of older bonds with lower coupons fall. An investor who holds such a bond to maturity notices nothing of this. If they have to sell before then, they realise the loss.

In the years of low interest rates, banks had taken in deposits at practically 0% and invested them long term, because short maturities yielded nothing. From 2022, central banks raised interest rates in one of the fastest rate cycles of the post-war period. As a result, this maturity transformation opened up a gap in the balance sheets. It was not hidden, as it appeared as an *unrealised loss* in the notes to the financial statements. Under US rules, however, these losses did not have to be booked through the income statement for securities intended to be held to maturity.

bloecke.formel: Price change ≈ − Modified duration × Change in interest rates
bloecke.erklaerung: This rule of thumb estimates the price loss of a bond or bond fund when interest rates rise. It applies to small changes in interest rates. With large jumps in rates, the loss turns out somewhat smaller because of convexity.
variablen: interest rate sensitivity in years, stated in the factsheet of every bond ETF
change in the market yield in percentage points
bloecke.beispiel: A fund with a modified duration of 7 loses around 21% of its market value when interest rates rise by 3 percentage points, even though not a single borrower has defaulted.

bloecke.md: At the end of 2022, Silicon Valley Bank had over $15 billion in unrealised losses on its books, with a balance sheet total of $209 billion. The liabilities side was decisive. Of its roughly $175 billion in deposits, around nine tenths were not covered by deposit protection, and these customers had a strong incentive to be the first to withdraw their money. On 8 March 2023, the bank announced that it had sold bonds worth $21 billion at an after-tax loss of $1.8 billion and intended to raise new equity. The sale had turned the book loss into a realised loss. On 9 March, customers then withdrew $42 billion in a single day. On 10 March, the bank was closed. It was the third-largest bank failure in US history. Two days later Signature Bank followed, with around $88.6 billion in deposits, and on 1 May First Republic, which was sold to JPMorgan for $10.6 billion. Across the entire US banking system, unrealised losses at the time added up to over $600 billion. On 12 March, the Fed launched the Bank Term Funding Program. It lent banks money against bonds, which were counted as collateral at face value instead of market value. This meant the banks did not have to sell their bonds at a loss and gained the time that Silicon Valley Bank had lacked.

bloecke.titel: Default risk and interest rate risk
bloecke.md: Default risk and interest rate risk are two different risks, and with a German federal bond only the first one disappears. A bond that will certainly be repaid at maturity can show a double-digit loss in the meantime. That does not matter as long as the investor decides when to sell. It becomes a threat to survival when the time of sale is dictated from outside: by customers who want their money back, by a broker making a margin call, or by a personal situation in which the savings buffer is needed immediately.

Credit Suisse failed for a different reason. Its problems did not lie with the yield curve. Reputational damage had accumulated at the bank: the Archegos loss of around CHF 5 billion, the Greensill affair and a net loss of CHF 7.3 billion for 2022. Customers withdrew CHF 110.5 billion in the fourth quarter of 2022 and a further 61.2 billion in the first quarter of 2023. In March 2023, outflows at times reached CHF 10 to 17 billion a day. On 19 March, UBS took over the bank, founded in 1856, for CHF 3 billion, paid in its own shares. The Swiss National Bank backed the takeover with two liquidity commitments of up to CHF 100 billion each.

For investors, what happened next is particularly instructive. Subordinated AT1 bonds worth CHF 16 billion were written down completely to zero, while the shareholders still received UBS shares. This reversed the usual order of loss absorption (first equity, then debt). The Swiss financial market supervisor FINMA based the write-down on a clause in the bond terms and on Swiss emergency law. In October 2025, the Swiss Federal Administrative Court ruled that the conditions of the clause had not been met and that the emergency law did not provide a sufficient legal basis either. The ruling is not final; FINMA and UBS have appealed to the Swiss Federal Supreme Court. Investors who buy subordinated bonds for their higher coupons thus also take on the risk of such a write-down.

bloecke.md: In 1931, a bank run dragged on for days, and customers had to queue at the counter. In 2023, it took only hours, and a chat group and a banking app were enough. Regulation after 2008 increased capital and liquidity buffers. However, it was not designed for a situation in which just under a quarter of deposits can flow out in a single day.

## Concentration in stock indices

The second finding of these years concerns stock indices. In 2026, the five largest technology companies accounted for around 30% of the S&P 500. That is the highest degree of concentration in half a century. In the MSCI World, the standard building block of German portfolios, the ten largest companies together accounted for 26.61% at the end of August 2026. An index fund covering 23 developed markets is therefore less broadly diversified than its name suggests. Diversification also decreases when the largest constituents rise the most.

bloecke.titel: The ten largest constituents of the MSCI World, as of 31 August 2026
bloecke.unter: The five largest companies together make up 19.4% of the index, the ten largest 26.6%, and all other constituents together just under three quarters.

bloecke.md:
The concentration is a consequence of the wave of investment in artificial intelligence. An index fund reflects the valuations of the stock market, and at present the stock market is valuing computing power above all. Whether these investments will pay off economically is an open question that cannot be decided with today's figures. The spending on data centres, chips and energy is incurred immediately, while the returns from it lie in the future. The same constellation (a real technology with unclear profitability) characterised internet shares in 1999 and railways in the 1870s. In both cases the technology prevailed. The losses fell on investors who wanted to be in at any price.

Valuation ratios are correspondingly high. The Shiller P/E of the S&P 500 relates the price to the inflation-adjusted ten-year average of earnings. On 18 September 2026 it stood at 40.94. The historical average is 17.42, and the record of 44.19 dates from December 1999. For the semiconductor sector, Damodaran gives a trailing P/E of 100.2 and a forward P/E of 37.3 for January 2026. The gap between the two figures results from the expected rise in earnings, which has yet to materialise.

Three differences can be documented. None of them is a reason to sound the all-clear.

The first difference concerns financing. The dotcom boom was financed through IPOs of loss-making companies and through debt. Today's big investors make money in their core business and pay for the investments largely out of operating cash flow. According to Kindleberger, the credit behind a bubble matters more than the story that accompanies it. Without leverage, the mechanism of forced selling is missing.

The second difference concerns the scale of possible losses. Because the companies finance their investments themselves, write-downs on them hit the profits of the largest index members directly. These members today account for a third of the US market, so they are not a fringe group.

The third difference concerns the sensitivity of the story on which the valuations rest. In January 2025, the news that a Chinese model achieved comparable performance with significantly less computing power was enough for Nvidia shares to lose 17% in one day. Earnings did not change that day. What changed was the assumption about how many chips would be needed in future.

For 2026 itself, the data are thin. The documented figures are a maximum decline of 9.1% in the S&P 500 within the year, between 27 January and 30 March, an all-time high of 7,798.99 points on 13 August and a closing level of 7,637.76 points on 17 September. Reports of a larger sell-off in semiconductor shares in the summer come from secondary sources and are therefore not presented here as fact.

## Interest rates and inflation in 2026

In 2026, the trend in inflation and interest rates reversed once again. With an annual average of 2.2% in Germany, 2025 was a year of disinflation. After that, the rise in prices picked up again, mainly because of energy prices. In August 2026, the German inflation rate was 2.9%. Energy became 10.5% more expensive, fuels 27.7%. The core rate excluding food and energy, by contrast, was only 2.4%. This is the textbook case of imported supply-side inflation, this time triggered by tensions in the Middle East. The ECB raised interest rates by 25 basis points on 10 September 2026, for the second time this year. The Federal Reserve followed on 16 September with a unanimous decision. It was its first rate rise since 2023.

bloecke.titel: Real interest rate on instant-access savings
bloecke.md:
€10,000 is held for one year in an instant-access savings account paying 2.2%. That yields €220 in interest.

Interest is income from capital assets under Section 20(1) no. 7 EStG (Income Tax Act). It is subject to the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) of 25% under Section 32d(1) EStG and to the solidarity surcharge, together 26.375% without church tax. If the saver's allowance (Sparer-Pauschbetrag) of €1,000 (€2,000 for joint assessment, Section 20(9) EStG) has already been used up by other income, €220 − €58.03 = €161.97 remains. That corresponds to 1.62% after tax.

With inflation at 2.9%, the €10,161.97 has purchasing power of around €9,875 in the previous year's prices. That is a real loss of about 1.2%. So in September 2026 there are positive interest rates again, but no positive real interest rate after tax.

## Recurring patterns and new developments

Central bank balance sheets have not returned to their starting point either. The Eurosystem has reduced its balance sheet from a peak of €8,836 billion (24 June 2022) to €5,911 billion by 11 September 2026. That is still around five times the level of early 2007. The Fed has already ended its balance sheet reduction. Its balance sheet reached its low of $6,536 billion on 3 December 2025, has been growing again since then and stood at $6,747 billion on 16 September 2026. So quantitative tightening is still under way in Europe, but no longer in the US. For interest rate forecasts, it therefore matters which of the two instruments is meant, the key interest rate or the size of the central bank balance sheet.

bloecke.md:
First, the modified duration of your bond allocation is stated in the factsheet. It lets you calculate in advance what a further rise in interest rates of one percentage point would cost.

Second, you can add up the weight of the largest individual holdings in your portfolio, each calculated as index weight times the fund's share of the portfolio, plus any direct holding. The total is often higher than expected.

Third, reserves that could be needed within twelve months belong in investments with a matching term. At Silicon Valley Bank the investments themselves were safe; the problem was their long maturity.

mitnehmen: Safety from default and price stability are two different properties, as shown by Silicon Valley Bank, which failed because of securities with no default risk.
The order of loss absorption in a crisis follows from the bond terms and can deviate from the textbook order; at Credit Suisse the AT1 creditors lost everything, the shareholders did not.
In 2026, a broad world index is less broadly diversified than its name suggests, as the ten largest constituents of the MSCI World accounted for 26.6% at the end of August.
Valuation ratios such as the Shiller P/E of 40.94 in September 2026 say something about the next ten years, but almost nothing about the next twelve months.

In 2026, positive interest rates do not mean a positive real interest rate, as 2.2% interest on instant-access savings results in a loss of purchasing power of around 1.2% after flat-rate withholding tax and with inflation at 2.9%.

begriffe.text: Risk that the price of a fixed-income security falls because market interest rates rise. It exists regardless of the creditworthiness of the debtor and only leads to a realised loss if the security has to be sold before maturity.
Measure of the interest rate sensitivity of a bond or bond fund. It indicates approximately by what percentage the price falls if the market yield rises by one percentage point.

Subordinated bank bond that counts as Additional Tier 1 capital for regulatory purposes. It can be written down or converted into shares if the capital ratio falls below a specified level or the supervisor orders it. At Credit Suisse, such bonds worth CHF 16 billion were written off completely in 2023.
Risk arising from the high weight of a few individual securities or sectors. In market-capitalisation-weighted indices it grows automatically when the largest constituents rise the most.

Reduction of a central bank's securities holdings, usually by not replacing maturing securities. It withdraws central bank money from the banking system and acts alongside the key interest rate as a second, slower instrument of monetary policy.
